title: Must and need
intro: This unit is about obligation and need. `-mAlY` says what someone must, has to or should do, and like the future in `-jAk` it takes no personal ending: *Men gitmeli*, I must go. *gerek* says what someone needs: *Maňa suw gerek*, I need water. And with *bolmak*, `-mAlY` moves into other tenses: *gitmeli boldum*, I had to go. Along the way: aches and pains, the doctor, and the signs that say what you mustn't do.

blocks.text: Add `-mAlY` to the stem: *-maly* after a back vowel, *-meli* after a front one. *git-* → *gitmeli*, *oka-* → *okamaly*. Like the future in `-jAk` ([A2 unit 3](a2-u03)), it takes **no personal ending**: the same word serves every person, so the subject has to be said. *Men gitmeli*, I must go; *Sen gitmeli*, you must go.

rows.en: I must go, I have to go
he, she or it must go

blocks.text: `-mAlY` starts with a consonant, so stems keep their shape: *git-* keeps its *t* (*gitmeli*), a stem's final *e* stays *e* (*işlemeli*, *tölemeli*). It covers **must**, **have to**, **should** and **need to**; the situation decides how strong it is. *Sen dynç almaly*, you should rest, you need to rest.

**Negative.** Put *däl* after it: *Men gitmeli däl*. It usually means **mustn't** or **shouldn't**: *Sen bu ýerde çilim çekmeli däl*, you mustn't smoke here. In context it can also mean **don't have to**; for a clear **no need**, use *gerek däl* (next section). You will also see the negative made with *-mA*, *gitmemeli*; this course writes *gitmeli däl*.

rows.en: I mustn't go, I shouldn't go
he, she or it mustn't go

blocks.text: **Questions.** Write `-mY` onto it: *Men gitmelimi?*, should I go? do I have to go? In the negative, the particle goes on *däl*: *gitmeli dälmi?* With a question word, no particle: *Men näme etmeli?*, what should I do? *Biz haçan gitmeli?*, when do we have to go?

rows.en: Must I go? Should I go?
Must he, she or it go?

items.en: I have to go to the doctor.
We have to get up early tomorrow.

items.tk: Sen bu ýerde çilim çekmeli däl.
items.seg: Sen bu ýer|de çilim çek|meli däl.

blocks.text: **Without a subject**, `-mAlY` states a general rule, **one must**, **you have to**: *Bu ýerde aýakgaby çykarmaly*, shoes have to come off here. So for **I must go**, say *Men gitmeli*: on its own, *Gitmeli* sounds like **one must go, it's time to go**.

blocks.title: No ending, but a subject
blocks.text: Don't add an ending: `gitmeliýin` and `gitmelim` are not forms. And say who: *Men gitmeli*, *Merdan gitmeli*. In the negative, *däl* is a separate word: *gitmeli däl*.

*gerek* means **needed, necessary**. The thing needed is the subject, and the person who needs it goes in the **dative**: *Maňa suw gerek*, I need water, literally **to me water is needed**. *gerek* itself never changes.

*gerek däl* is **not needed**: *Maňa kömek gerek däl*, I don't need help. On its own, *Gerek däl!* means **no need!**, a polite way to refuse an offer. Ask with *gerekmi?*: *Saňa kömek gerekmi?*, do you need help?

After an infinitive in `-mAk`, *gerek* gives a general **one should, you need to**: *Ir turmak gerek*, one should get up early; *Köp suw içmek gerek*, you need to drink a lot of water. For a particular person, use `-mAlY`: *Men ir turmaly*.

*hökman* adds force: **definitely, without fail**. With `-mAlY` it means **really must**: *Sen hökman lukmana gitmeli*. With an imperative: *Ertir hökman gel!*, be sure to come tomorrow! *Hökman däl* is **not compulsory**.

items.en: I have a headache; I need some medicine.
We don't need a new car.

blocks.title: Where does it hurt?
blocks.text: *agyrmak* is **to hurt, to ache**, and what hurts takes a possessive: *Başym agyrýar*, I have a headache (my head hurts); *Dişim agyrýar*, I have toothache; *Garnym agyrýar*, I have a stomach ache. *garyn* loses its second vowel before a vowel ending, like *burun* → *burnum* ([A1 unit 9](a1-u09)).

blocks.title: The dative, not the subject
blocks.text: **I need** is *Maňa … gerek*, not `Men … gerek`: the person goes in the dative. And *gerek* takes no ending: *Bize gerek*, not `Bize gerekis`.

sections.title: I had to, I'll have to

blocks.text: `-mAlY` on its own talks about now: *Men gitmeli*, I must go. To put it in another tense, add *bolmak* and give *bolmak* the tense and the ending: *gitmeli boldum*, I had to go; *gitmeli bolaryn*, I'll have to go; *gitmeli bolýar*, she has to go (these days, regularly).

rows.en: he, she or it had to go
you had to go (plural or polite)

blocks.caption: -mAlY with bolmak
head: Turkmen
Meaning
rows: I must go, I have to go (now).
I have to go (regularly, these days).

blocks.text: Because *bolmak* carries the ending, the pronoun can go when the ending says who: *Düýn işlemeli boldum*, I had to work yesterday. With *boljak*, as with any `-jAk`, keep the subject: *Men ertir işlemeli boljak*.

items.en: We had to wait for an hour.
We'll have to get up early tomorrow.
She has to work every day.

items.tk: Olar ýolda iki gün galmaly boldular.
items.seg: Olar ýol|da iki gün gal|maly bol|du|lar.
items.en: They had to stay on the road for two days.

blocks.title: Must has no past
blocks.text: English **must** has no past either: you switch to **had to**. Turkmen switches to *bolmak*: *gitmeli* becomes *gitmeli boldum*.

blocks.title: The ending goes on bolmak
blocks.text: *gitmeli boldum*, not `gitmelim boldum` or `gitmeli bolmaly`: `-mAlY` stays as it is, and *bolmak* takes the tense and the person.

summary: **Must, have to, should**: stem + `-mAlY` (*gitmeli, okamaly*), with no personal ending, so say who: *Men gitmeli*.
Negative *gitmeli däl* (mustn't, shouldn't); question *gitmelimi?*, *Men näme etmeli?*
**Need**: the person in the dative + *gerek*: *Maňa suw gerek*; *gerek däl*, *gerekmi?*; *Ir turmak gerek* (one should).
*hökman* (definitely, without fail): *Sen hökman gelmeli*, *Ertir hökman gel!*
Other tenses with *bolmak*: *gitmeli boldum* (had to), *gitmeli bolaryn* (will have to), *gitmeli bolýar* (has to, regularly).
